Quick answer: Swimming is beneficial for arthritis as water's buoyancy supports up to 90% of body weight, reducing joint load and pain. Warm water, ideally 28–32°C, relaxes muscles and increases blood flow, while hydrostatic pressure can reduce joint swelling. Regular sessions, starting with 15–20 minutes and building to 30–45 minutes, two to three times weekly, can improve physical function and quality of life.

Swimming for Arthritis: A Complete Guide

Swimming and aquatic exercise are among the most effective forms of physical activity for people with arthritis. The buoyancy of water supports up to 90% of your body weight, making movement easier and less painful.

Why Water Works

  • Buoyancy reduces joint loading by up to 90%
  • Warm water (28–32°C) relaxes muscles and increases blood flow
  • Hydrostatic pressure reduces swelling in joints
  • Resistance builds muscle strength without weights

What the Research Says

A 2023 Cochrane review of aquatic exercise for OA found:

  • Significant reductions in pain (moderate evidence)
  • Improved physical function (moderate evidence)
  • Enhanced quality of life (low-moderate evidence)
  • Benefits comparable to land-based exercise

Best Swimming Strokes for Arthritis

Stroke Best For Avoid If
Backstroke Shoulder, hip, knee OA Neck problems
Breaststroke General fitness Knee OA (modified kick)
Front crawl Upper body strength Shoulder impingement
Aqua walking All types, beginners —

Getting Started

  1. Find a warm pool — hydrotherapy pools (33–36°C) are ideal but standard heated pools (28–30°C) work too
  2. Start with 15–20 minutes and build to 30–45 minutes
  3. Aim for 2–3 sessions per week
  4. Try aqua aerobics — structured classes with instructor guidance
  5. Use a float if needed for support

UK Pool Resources

  • Swim England — find pools near you with disability-friendly facilities
  • NHS hydrotherapy — ask your GP or physiotherapist for a referral
  • Versus Arthritis — local groups often organise warm water sessions
  • Everyone Active / Better Leisure — concession rates for people with disabilities

Tips for Comfort

  • Shower in warm water before entering the pool
  • Use neoprene gloves if hands are affected
  • Avoid cold pools (below 26°C)
  • Stretch gently after your session
  • Apply moisturiser — chlorine can dry skin

Written by Mark Thompson, Aquatic Physiotherapist, NHS

Practical next steps for Swimming for Arthritis: A Complete Guide

If you came here about Swimming for Arthritis: A Complete Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Quick questions about Swimming Arthritis Complete Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on swimming for arthritis: a complete guide. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.
